title: Interactive Debugger - public implementations survey
definition: Allows execution to be paused and inspected.
description:
Interactive Debugger is one of the fundamental capabilities an AI needs to build things on demand: Allows execution to be paused and inspected. In the real world this capability is delivered by a rich ecosystem of tools, libraries and platforms. This database is the public edition - a fact-checked survey of the real implementations, the real techniques they share, the standards they follow, and laddered drills that teach the capability hands-on.

No single tool owns Interactive Debugger. Competing implementations emphasize different trade-offs: speed against flexibility, simplicity against power, integration against independence. The implementation spotlights in this database document the notable real ones - what each does, where it excels, and how it serves Interactive Debugger. Together they map the territory as it actually exists.

Every record carries a runnable demonstration program, because tools are understood by use. Run the demos with node, compare the implementations, practice the drills, and the Interactive Debugger capability becomes something you can reach for - with full knowledge of which real tool fits which job.

t: Chrome DevTools - related Interactive Debugger technology
title: Chrome DevTools - related Interactive Debugger technology
definition: The everyday browser debugger.
description:
Chrome DevTools is not itself an Interactive Debugger, but it belongs in this survey because real Interactive Debugger work leans on it. The everyday browser debugger.

In an Interactive Debugger build it shows up when the team already lives in its ecosystem. The design favors boring reliability over cleverness: well-trodden paths, clear errors, and behavior you can reason about without reading the source. Knowing the surrounding technology is part of knowing the capability - the best Interactive Debugger practitioners can say exactly where their tool ends and its neighbors begin.

For builders, Chrome DevTools is worth evaluating first as supporting technology. The demo program exercises a core idea from its domain - run it with node and watch each step.

t: Interactive Debugger definition of done - practitioner discipline
title: Interactive Debugger definition of done - practitioner discipline
definition: The definition of done discipline for Interactive Debugger: allows execution to be paused and inspected..
description:
definition of done is the Interactive Debugger discipline: Allows execution to be paused and inspected. It turns Interactive Debugger from an event into a repeatable capability.

In practice this means: log every decision with its reason, so the next builder inherits understanding; verify outputs against the original request, not against your hopes; keep a failure log: what broke, why, and what now prevents it Teams that follow the discipline get predictable builds; teams that skip it get interesting stories. The Signature line prefers predictable builds, and this record's demo makes the discipline concrete and runnable.

Good Interactive Debugger practice is not talent - it is handoff protocol. It turns Interactive Debugger from an event into a repeatable capability.

Concretely: verify outputs against the original request, not against your hopes; keep a failure log: what broke, why, and what now prevents it; review the result with fresh eyes before calling it done This record exists because the difference between a tool and a capability is discipline. Run the demo, adopt the checklist, and Interactive Debugger becomes something your builds can rely on.

t: Foundation drill - name the inputs, outputs, and contracts of Interactive Debug
title: Foundation drill - name the inputs, outputs, and contracts of Interactive Debug
definition: Ladder drill (foundation): name the inputs, outputs, and contracts of Interactive Debugger from a one-paragraph brief.
description:
Drill (FOUNDATION): name the inputs, outputs, and contracts of Interactive Debugger from a one-paragraph brief

Read the brief twice. List every input the Interactive Debugger needs, every output it must produce, and one contract each input-output pair must satisfy. Work it by hand first, then run the demo program and compare its trace against your own reasoning. When they agree, the concept is yours.

Success criterion: you can list them from memory without looking at the brief
